maths_aqa_f.5.1.summary: Data presentation is a foundational skill in AQA GCSE Maths, transforming raw measurements into clear, visual representations. This topic covers the accurate construction and interpretation of tally charts, two-way tables, pictograms, bar charts, pie charts, stem and leaf diagrams, and time series graphs. Mastering these methods requires precise calculations—such as sector angles for pie charts—alongside strict presentation standards including clear keys, uniform axis scales, and ordered data layouts.

core.p: Tally charts are designed to gather raw discrete or continuous data efficiently by recording tallies in groups of five. The fifth mark is drawn diagonally across four vertical lines to facilitate quick counting into a final frequency column.
bullets: **Tally Marks**: Single vertical strokes for 1 to 4; a diagonal line across four strokes represents 5.
**Frequency Column**: The total count for each category, obtained by summing the tallies.
**Ungrouped Data**: Used for distinct categories or small integer sets (e.g., shoe sizes).
**Grouped Data**: Used for continuous data or large ranges; data is sorted into non-overlapping class intervals (e.g., 0 < t ≤ 10).

callouts.p: The total number of times a specific data value or category occurs within a data set.
Ensure class intervals do not overlap. Writing 0–10 and 10–20 creates ambiguity for the value 10. Write 0 < t ≤ 10 and 10 < t ≤ 20 instead.

core.p: Two-way tables display frequencies for two categorical variables simultaneously, organized into rows and columns. They allow quick cross-referencing and calculation of totals across subgroups.
bullets: **Row and Column Totals**: Every row and column must sum to its respective marginal total.
**Grand Total**: The bottom-right cell represents the overall sample size (N), equal to the sum of all row totals and the sum of all column totals.
**Problem Solving**: Missing values are found by working backwards from known totals using basic subtraction.

callouts.p: Always verify that your row totals and column totals both add up to the grand total in the bottom-right corner.

core.p: Pictograms represent frequency using repeated visual symbols or icons. A crucial element of any pictogram is its key, which defines the numerical quantity represented by a single full symbol.
bullets: **Key Requirement**: Must explicitly state what one full symbol represents (e.g., 1 circle = 4 students).
**Partial Symbols**: Half or quarter symbols represent fractional frequencies. For example, half a symbol represents 2 students if a full symbol represents 4.
**Proportional Layout**: Symbols must be drawn at a uniform size and aligned neatly in columns or rows to enable visual comparison.

callouts.p: A pictogram without a key loses all quantitative meaning and will lose marks in an AQA exam.

core.p: Bar charts display categorical or discrete data using rectangular bars where the length or height of each bar is proportional to its frequency.
bullets: **Equal Gaps**: Clear, uniform spaces must separate adjacent bars (unlike histograms).
**Uniform Scale**: The vertical axis (frequency) must start at 0 and increase by constant intervals.
**Labeling**: Both axes must be clearly labeled with units where appropriate, and each bar must be labeled.

callouts.p: Bars must have identical widths and equal spacing between them. Drawing touching bars for categorical data is penalized.

core.p: Dual bar charts place two or more bars side by side for each category, allowing direct comparison between two distinct sub-groups (such as boys vs. girls or Year 2022 vs. Year 2023).
bullets: **Paired Bars**: Bars for the same category touch each other.
**Category Spacing**: A clear gap must separate the clusters of paired bars for different categories.
**Shading and Key**: Distinct shading, colors, or hatching must be used for each sub-group, accompanied by a clear key.

callouts.p: In black-and-white exam papers, differentiate paired bars using distinct shading styles (e.g., solid vs. diagonal lines).

core.p: Composite bar charts show the total frequency for a category as a single bar, with sub-categories stacked vertically on top of one another within that bar.
bullets: **Total Height**: The top of the entire bar represents the total frequency of that category.
**Segment Frequency**: Calculated by taking the upper value of a segment and subtracting its lower boundary value.
**Key & Legend**: Color or shading differentiates the stacked components.

callouts.p: Do not read the height of an upper segment directly off the y-axis. Calculate: Segment Height = Top Reading − Bottom Reading.

core.p: Pie charts visually display the relative proportions of a dataset as sectors of a full circle (360 degrees).
bullets: **Total Frequency Formula**: Sum all frequencies to find the grand total (N).
**Multiplier**: Compute the angle per unit of frequency using multiplier = 360 / N.
**Sector Angle Formula**: Sector Angle = Frequency × (360 / N).
**Angle Check**: The sum of all calculated sector angles must equal exactly 360°.

callouts.p: The interior angle at the center of a pie chart representing a specific category's fraction of the total data.

core.p: Accurate drawing requires a protractor, ruler, and sharp pencil. Interpretation involves converting sector angles back into frequencies or comparing proportions across charts.
bullets: **Drawing Step 1**: Draw a vertical radius from the center straight up to 12 o'clock.
**Drawing Step 2**: Measure the first sector angle using a protractor placed at the center.
**Drawing Step 3**: Draw the boundary line, then measure the next angle from this new line.
**Comparing Pie Charts**: Pie charts compare relative proportions, not absolute quantities, unless total frequencies for both charts are known to be equal.

callouts.p: A larger sector in Pie Chart A does not mean a higher frequency than in Pie Chart B if the total sample sizes of A and B differ.

core.p: Stem and leaf diagrams organize numerical data into order while preserving every original raw data value.
bullets: **Structure**: The 'Stem' represents leading digits (tens, hundreds), and the 'Leaf' represents the trailing single digit (units).
**Ordering**: Leaves in every row must be listed in ascending order from left to right with equal spacing.
**Mandatory Key**: Must state how stem and leaf combine to give a data value (e.g., 2 | 5 means 25).
**Averages**: Useful for finding the median (middle position (n+1)/2), mode (most frequent leaf), and range (maximum − minimum).

callouts.t: Exam Rule for Stem & Leaf Diagrams
callouts.p: Always provide a fully labeled key including units. Without a key, full marks cannot be awarded.

core.p: Back-to-back stem and leaf diagrams allow direct comparison of two distributions (e.g., Class A vs Class B) using a single central stem.
bullets: **Central Stem**: Shared down the middle column.
**Left-side Leaves**: Written in reverse order, increasing outwards from right to left.
**Right-side Leaves**: Written in standard order, increasing outwards from left to right.
**Dual Key**: Must provide a key explaining how to read data from both the left and right sides.

callouts.p: Be careful when reading the left side: 3 | 2 means 23 if 2 is on the left leaf and 3 is in the central stem.

core.p: Time series graphs display data recorded sequentially over regular time intervals (e.g., hours, months, years) to visualize trends and cyclical patterns over time.
bullets: **Axes Layout**: Time is always plotted on the horizontal x-axis; the measured variable is on the vertical y-axis.
**Plotting Points**: Each data point is plotted accurately at its specific time step.
**Line Segments**: Plotted points must be joined using straight line segments drawn with a ruler (do not draw smooth curves).
**Reading Values**: Interpolate between points or read exact recorded points along the line.

callouts.p: In AQA GCSE time series graphs, points must be connected with straight lines. Curved lines will result in lost marks.

core.h: Trends and Variations in Time Series
core.p: Analyzing a time series graph involves recognizing overall long-term direction as well as regular, repeating short-term fluctuations.
bullets: **General Trend**: The overall direction of data over a long period—upward (increasing), downward (decreasing), or flat (constant).
**Trend Line**: A straight line of best fit drawn through the middle of the time series fluctuations to indicate general direction.
**Seasonal Variation**: Regular, predictable peaks and troughs repeating at specific intervals (e.g., high ice cream sales every summer, low sales in winter).

callouts.p: A repetitive pattern of predictable increases or decreases occurring within regular intervals of time, such as daily, quarterly, or annually.

core.p: Vertical line diagrams are used to represent discrete numerical data, functioning similarly to bar charts but utilizing single vertical lines instead of wide bars.
bullets: **Discrete Data Focus**: Well-suited for discrete quantities like score frequencies or counts of items per household.
**Line Heights**: The length/height of each line is directly proportional to the frequency of that numerical value.
**Spacing**: Vertical lines are placed at uniform intervals along the horizontal axis corresponding to the discrete data values.

callouts.p: If an exam question specifies a 'vertical line diagram', draw thin vertical lines using a ruler rather than wide bars.

analogy.p: Statistical charts and diagrams act like different lenses on a camera. A two-way table acts like a wide-angle grid lens, organizing complex multi-variable information into structured rows and columns. A time series graph acts like a time-lapse camera, capturing movement, trends, and seasonal rhythms across time. A pie chart acts like a circular aperture, revealing how a single complete picture is divided into fractional slices. However, like any camera lens, charts can distort reality if scales are broken, labels are missing, or sample sizes are ignored.

mistakes.w: Omitting the key from a stem and leaf diagram or pictogram.
mistakes.r: Always include a clear key, such as '1 | 5 = 15 marks' or '1 circle = 4 items'.

mistakes.w: Drawing touching bars on a standard bar chart.
mistakes.r: Leave equal gaps between adjacent bars when presenting categorical or discrete data.

mistakes.w: Calculating pie chart angles using 360 divided by frequency instead of total frequency.
mistakes.r: Calculate angle = (frequency / total frequency) × 360.

mistakes.w: Assuming a larger pie chart sector always means a larger absolute frequency when comparing two pie charts.
mistakes.r: Proportions can only be converted to absolute numbers if the total sample sizes of both pie charts are known.

mistakes.w: Connecting time series data points with smooth curves.
mistakes.r: Join time series data points using straight line segments drawn with a ruler.

mistakes.w: Listing leaves in unsorted order in a stem and leaf diagram.
mistakes.r: Always order leaves in ascending numerical order from left to right.

mistakes.w: Reading stacked bar chart segment values straight off the y-axis.
mistakes.r: Subtract the lower boundary reading of the segment from its upper boundary reading.

mistakes.w: Writing overlapping class boundaries like 0–10 and 10–20.
mistakes.r: Use precise inequality notation such as 0 < t ≤ 10 and 10 < t ≤ 20.

exam.q: A pictogram key shows that 1 full circle represents 8 books. State how many books are represented by 3 full circles and 3/4 of a circle.
exam.tip: Break down whole symbols and partial symbols separately before adding them.

exam.q:
Complete the missing entries in this two-way table:
- Boys: 12 Walk, 15 Bus, Total = 27
- Girls: [?] Walk, 9 Bus, Total = 22
- Total: [?] Walk, 24 Bus, Grand Total = 49
model: Girls Walk = 22 Total - 9 Bus = 13 Girls Walk.
Total Walk = 12 Boys + 13 Girls = 25 Total Walk.
exam.tip: Work backwards from known row or column totals to find missing entries.

exam.q: A survey of 60 people shows 15 prefer Tea, 25 prefer Coffee, and 20 prefer Water. Calculate the sector angle for Coffee in a pie chart.
exam.tip: Check your answer by calculating all angles (90°, 150°, 120°) and verifying they sum to 360°.

exam.q: Construct an ordered stem and leaf diagram with a key for the following test scores: 23, 14, 35, 23, 41, 19, 28, 35, 32.
exam.tip: First construct an unordered draft diagram, then re-write it cleanly in ascending order.

exam.q: A pie chart represents 120 students. The sector angle for Art is 54°. Calculate the number of students who chose Art.
exam.tip: Divide the angle by 360 to find the proportion, then multiply by total students.

exam.q: Describe the general trend and seasonal variation shown in a time series graph of ice cream sales recorded quarterly over 3 years.
model: General trend: Sales show an overall upward/increasing trend over the 3 years.
Seasonal variation: Sales consistently peak in Q3 (summer) and drop to lowest points in Q1 (winter) each year.
exam.tip: Separate your answer into two distinct points: overall trend line movement and repetitive annual cycles.

exam.q: Explain why a pie chart showing 40% preference for Football in School A (1000 pupils) does not mean fewer pupils like Football than in School B where Football has a 50% sector angle (200 pupils).
model: School A: 40% of 1000 = 400 pupils prefer Football.
School B: 50% of 200 = 100 pupils prefer Football.
Pie charts show proportions, not total quantities; School A has more pupils choosing Football despite a smaller percentage.
exam.tip: Calculate actual numbers when total sample sizes are provided to compare quantities accurately.

exam.q:
Find the median value from this ordered stem and leaf diagram:
1 | 2 5 8
2 | 1 3 4 7
3 | 0 2
Key: 1 | 2 = 12
model: Counting leaves in order: 12, 15, 18, 21, 23 → 5th item is 23.
exam.tip: Count values in order from top-left to bottom-right to locate the median position.

exam.q:
Draw a dual bar chart to represent the following data for two clubs: 
Club A: Mon = 10, Tue = 15, Wed = 20
Club B: Mon = 12, Tue = 8, Wed = 16
List the criteria needed for full marks.
model: Linear vertical scale starting at 0 with equal steps labeled up to at least 20.
Equal width paired bars with Club A and Club B bars touching for each day.
Clear gaps between the day categories on the horizontal axis.
Accurate key or shading differentiating Club A and Club B.
exam.tip: Use a ruler and pencil. Ensure categories are clearly separated.

worked.q: In a school of 180 students, data on transportation was collected: 45 walk, 60 ride a bus, 30 cycle, and 45 get a car ride. Calculate the sector angles and describe how to draw the pie chart.
steps: Step 1: Calculate the multiplier (degrees per student). Multiplier = 360° ÷ 180 = 2° per student.
Step 2: Calculate each sector angle: Walk = 45 × 2° = 90°; Bus = 60 × 2° = 120°; Cycle = 30 × 2° = 60°; Car = 45 × 2° = 90°.
Step 3: Verify the sum of angles: 90° + 120° + 60° + 90° = 360°.

Step 4: Drawing instructions: Draw a circle with a compass and mark the vertical baseline at 12 o'clock. Use a protractor to measure 90° for Walk, then measure 120° from the new line for Bus, 60° for Cycle, and the remaining 90° for Car. Label all sectors clearly.
worked.ans: Sector angles: Walk = 90°, Bus = 120°, Cycle = 60°, Car = 90°.

worked.q: The following data shows the temperature (°C) recorded at 12:00 PM over 7 consecutive days: 14, 16, 15, 18, 17, 21, 20. Construct a time series line graph layout and describe how to identify the general trend.
steps: Step 1: Set up axes: Horizontal x-axis = Days (Day 1 to Day 7); Vertical y-axis = Temperature (°C) scaled from 12°C to 22°C in steps of 2°C.
Step 3: Connect consecutive points using straight line segments drawn with a ruler.
Step 4: Identify trend: Observe that overall temperature increases from Day 1 (14°C) to Day 7 (20°C). Draw a straight dashed line of best fit through the points showing a clear positive slope.
worked.ans: Graph plotted with straight line segments showing a general upward trend in temperature.

maths_aqa_f.5.2.summary: In AQA GCSE Maths Foundation tier, statistics questions on grouped data focus on histograms with equal class widths and grouped frequency tables. Unlike Higher tier where unequal class widths require frequency density and cumulative frequency curves are drawn, Foundation tier histograms use frequency directly on the vertical axis because all class intervals are of equal size. Master how to read, draw, and interpret equal-width histograms, identify the modal class, and calculate estimated means from grouped frequency tables.

core.h: 1. Grouped Continuous Data and Class Intervals
core.p: When dealing with continuous data such as height, mass, or time, individual data points are collected and grouped into intervals called **class intervals**. This makes large data sets manageable and easy to analyse.
bullets: **Continuous data** can take any numerical value within a range (e.g. time, weight, length).
**Class intervals** group data using inequality notation such as 0 < t ≤ 10, meaning greater than 0 up to and including 10.
At **Foundation tier**, class intervals in histograms are always of **equal width** (e.g. 0 to 10, 10 to 20, 20 to 30).
Equal class widths mean that the frequency of each interval is directly represented by the height of the bar.

callouts.p: A range of values used to group continuous data in a table or graph, defined by a lower bound and an upper bound.

core.h: 2. Key Features of Equal Width Histograms
core.p: A histogram with equal class widths looks similar to a bar chart, but it represents continuous data along a continuous scale with no gaps between the bars.
bullets: **Vertical Axis (Y-axis)** represents **Frequency** on the Foundation tier because all bars have equal widths.
**Horizontal Axis (X-axis)** represents a continuous numerical scale (e.g. Mass in kg, Time in seconds).
**No Gaps Between Bars**: Because the data is continuous, the end of one bar is the exact start of the next bar.
**Bar Height**: The height of each bar is equal to the frequency of that class interval.

callouts.p: On Foundation tier papers, the y-axis of a histogram is always labelled 'Frequency'. You do NOT use 'Frequency Density' unless studying Higher tier.

core.p: Understanding the dimensions of class intervals is crucial for interpreting grouped frequency tables and drawing histograms.
bullets: **Class Width Formula**: Class Width = Upper Bound − Lower Bound.
Example for interval 10 < x ≤ 25: Class Width = 25 − 10 = 15.
**Class Midpoint Formula**: Midpoint = (Lower Bound + Upper Bound) ÷ 2.
Example for interval 10 < x ≤ 25: Midpoint = (10 + 25) ÷ 2 = 17.5.
In **equal class width histograms**, every single row in the frequency table has the exact same class width value.

callouts.p: Always check the width of every interval in a table. If all widths are equal, you can plot frequencies directly as bar heights on the y-axis.

core.h: 4. Drawing Equal Class Width Histograms Step-by-Step
core.p: Follow a strict procedure when asked to draw a histogram for continuous data on an AQA Foundation exam paper.
bullets: **Step 1: Check class widths**: Confirm all class intervals in the table have equal widths.
**Step 2: Choose scales**: Use a linear scale for the vertical axis (Frequency) that fits the maximum frequency.
**Step 3: Label axes**: Clearly label the horizontal axis with the quantity and units, and vertical axis as 'Frequency'.
**Step 4: Draw bars**: Draw rectangular bars touching each other with no gaps. Ensure bar edges line up with class interval bounds on the x-axis.
**Step 5: Use a ruler**: Draw straight, clean lines. Imprecise hand-drawn lines lose marks.

callouts.p: Leaving gaps between bars in a histogram of continuous data is one of the most common ways students lose marks on AQA papers.

core.p: Extracting information from an equal-width histogram involves reading bar heights accurately.
bullets: **Frequency of an Interval**: Read the height of the bar corresponding to that interval on the vertical axis.
**Total Sample Size (N)**: Add together the heights of all the bars in the histogram.
**Frequency Above/Below a Value**: Identify bars that fall above or below the target value and sum their heights.
**Example**: If bars have heights 4, 9, 12, and 5, the total number of items recorded is 4 + 9 + 12 + 5 = 30.

callouts.p: Check the grid square values on the y-axis. If 10 small squares equal 5 units, each small square represents 0.5 units.

core.p: The modal class is the class interval containing the highest frequency of data points.
bullets: **Definition**: The modal class is the interval that occurs most frequently.
**On a Histogram**: Look for the tallest bar in the diagram.
**Writing the Answer**: State the full class interval (e.g. '20 < t ≤ 30'), NOT just the frequency or single numbers.
**Do not confuse with mode**: Mode refers to a single value in discrete data; modal class refers to an interval in grouped data.

callouts.p: The class interval with the highest frequency in a grouped frequency distribution.

core.h: 7. Estimating the Mean from Grouped Data
core.p: Because individual raw data values are lost when data is grouped into intervals, we calculate an **estimate** of the mean using class midpoints.
bullets: **Step 1**: Find the midpoint (m) of each class interval.
**Step 2**: Multiply each midpoint by its corresponding frequency (f × m).
**Step 3**: Sum all the (f × m) products to get Total (f × m).
**Step 4**: Sum all frequencies to get Total Frequency (Σf).
**Step 5**: Divide Total (f × m) by Total Frequency (Σf): Estimated Mean = Σ(f × m) ÷ Σf.
**Why is it an estimate?**: We assume all data values in an interval are equal to the midpoint of that interval.

callouts.p: Always write 'Estimated Mean' when asked why the calculated mean is not exact. State that the exact original values within intervals are unknown.

core.p: Understanding the visual and mathematical differences between bar charts and histograms prevents common diagrammatic errors.
bullets: **Bar Charts**: Used for discrete or categorical data (e.g. favourite color, shoe size). Gaps are left between bars.
**Equal-Width Histograms**: Used for continuous numerical data (e.g. height, time, mass). No gaps between bars.
**Axis Labels**: Bar charts have category names on the x-axis; histograms have a continuous numerical number line.
**Foundation Tier Equivalence**: When class widths are equal, bar height is proportional to frequency in both diagrams.

core.h: 9. Understanding Inequality Notation in Class Intervals
core.p: Class intervals use inequality symbols to ensure every data value falls into exactly one interval without overlap.
bullets: **Notation 0 < x ≤ 10**: Means values strictly greater than 0, up to and including 10.
**Strict Inequality (<)**: Excludes the boundary value (e.g. x > 0 does not include 0).
**Inclusive Inequality (≤)**: Includes the boundary value (e.g. x ≤ 10 includes 10).
**Boundary values**: A data value of exactly 10 goes into 0 < x ≤ 10, NOT into 10 < x ≤ 20.

callouts.p: For intervals 0 < x ≤ 10 and 10 < x ≤ 20, a value of 10 belongs to the first interval because of the '≤ 10' sign.

core.h: 10. Higher Tier Overview: Unequal Class Widths and Frequency Density
core.p: Understanding why Foundation tier uses equal class widths helps clarify the boundary between Foundation and Higher tier content.
bullets: **Unequal Class Widths**: Found on Higher tier papers. When class widths vary (e.g. 0 to 5, 5 to 20), bar height cannot equal frequency.
**Frequency Density Formula**: Frequency Density = Frequency ÷ Class Width.
**Area Represents Frequency**: On Higher tier unequal histograms, Area of bar = Frequency.
**Foundation Context**: At Foundation tier, class widths are always equal, so Frequency Density calculation is NOT required!

callouts.p: The frequency divided by the class width, used as the vertical axis scale when class widths are unequal.

core.h: 11. Higher Tier Overview: Cumulative Frequency Graphs
core.p: Cumulative frequency graphs are another Higher tier topic that relates to grouped data representation.
bullets: **Running Total**: Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies as you move through intervals.
**Plotting Points**: Plotted at the **upper boundary** of each class interval against the cumulative frequency.
**Curved Line**: Points are joined with a smooth S-shaped curve or straight line segments.
**Used For**: Estimating the median, lower quartile, upper quartile, and interquartile range (IQR).
**Foundation Tier Note**: You do NOT draw or interpret cumulative frequency graphs on Foundation papers.

callouts.p: On Foundation papers, if you see grouped data, you will be asked for equal-width histograms, grouped tables, modal class, or estimated mean—not cumulative frequency curves.

core.h: 12. Exam Problem-Solving Strategies for Foundation Statistics
core.p: Applying systematic methods when solving exam questions ensures maximum marks on histograms and grouped frequency tables.
bullets: **Check Axis Markings**: Count the small grid squares between major numbers on both axes before reading values.
**Show Calculations**: When calculating estimated mean, write out the table columns for Midpoint and (f × m).
**Check Reasonable Answers**: An estimated mean must fall within the range of the smallest and largest values in the table.
**Use Units**: Include correct units (e.g. cm, seconds, kg) in final numerical answers where requested.

callouts.p: If your estimated mean calculation gives 45 but all interval values are between 0 and 30, you made an arithmetic error. Re-check your division.

analogy.t: Building Blocks of Equal Width vs Custom Cut Blocks
analogy.p: Imagine building a set of steps using standardized Lego bricks of identical width. Because every brick is identical in width, the total height of a stack depends purely on the number of bricks (frequency) piled on top. This is like an equal-width histogram on Foundation tier: bar height directly equals frequency. The analogy breaks down if you use custom blocks of different widths (Higher tier unequal histograms), where wider blocks spread out the mass and force you to calculate density (height = area / width) rather than simply counting heights.

terms.d: A graphical representation of continuous numerical data using vertical touching bars where bar heights represent frequencies when class widths are equal.
A defined range of numerical values into which continuous data is grouped.
When every class interval in a frequency distribution has the exact same difference between its upper and lower boundaries.
The difference between the upper boundary and lower boundary of a class interval (Upper Limit - Lower Limit).
The central value of a class interval, calculated as (Lower Bound + Upper Bound) ÷ 2.
The total count of data items that fall within a specific class interval.
The class interval that has the highest frequency in a grouped frequency table or histogram.
An approximation of the mean average for grouped data, calculated using class midpoints multiplied by frequencies divided by total frequency.

Data that can only take specific, distinct values, such as shoe sizes or counts of people.

A running total of frequencies up to the upper limit of each class interval (Higher Tier only).
Mathematical symbols (<, >, ≤, ≥) used to define clear boundaries for class intervals without overlap.
The highest possible numerical value contained within a class interval.

mistakes.w: Leaving gaps between bars when drawing a histogram for continuous data.
mistakes.r: Draw bars touching each other with no gaps because the horizontal axis represents a continuous numerical scale.

mistakes.w: Writing just a single number (e.g. '12') for the modal class.
mistakes.r: State the full class interval (e.g. '10 < t ≤ 20') that has the highest frequency.

mistakes.w: Dividing total (f × m) by the number of rows in the table to find the estimated mean.
mistakes.r: Divide total (f × m) by total frequency (the sum of all frequencies, Σf).

mistakes.w: Calculating frequency density on a Foundation tier histogram question.
mistakes.r: Plot frequency directly on the vertical axis because Foundation tier histograms always have equal class widths.

mistakes.w: Using upper class limits instead of midpoints when estimating the mean.
mistakes.r: Use the exact midpoint of each interval: (Lower Bound + Upper Bound) ÷ 2.

mistakes.w: Plotting points for a bar chart on lines rather than centering bars over intervals.
mistakes.r: Draw rectangular bars extending from the exact lower bound to the exact upper bound along the continuous horizontal axis.

mistakes.w: Misreading axis grid scale values (e.g. assuming 1 small square = 1 unit when 5 squares = 2 units).
mistakes.r: Calculate the exact value per grid square before reading or plotting values.

mistakes.w: Assuming a cumulative frequency graph is required on Foundation tier.
mistakes.r: Recognise cumulative frequency curves are Higher tier content; Foundation tier tests equal-width histograms and grouped tables.

exam.q:
The table shows the time, t minutes, taken by 40 students to complete a test.
Time (t mins): 0 < t ≤ 10 (Freq: 5), 10 < t ≤ 20 (Freq: 12), 20 < t ≤ 30 (Freq: 15), 30 < t ≤ 40 (Freq: 8).
Write down the modal class.
exam.tip: Identify the highest frequency (15) and copy the exact interval notation given in the table.

exam.q:
A grouped frequency table has intervals 0 < x ≤ 10, 10 < x ≤ 20, 20 < x ≤ 30, and 30 < x ≤ 40.
State the class width of each interval.
exam.tip: Class width is upper bound minus lower bound: 10 - 0 = 10.

exam.q: Explain why a histogram representing continuous data has no gaps between its bars.
model: Because the data is continuous, so the end of one class interval is the start of the next interval.
exam.tip: Mention 'continuous data' or 'intervals touch' to earn the mark.

exam.q:
The frequencies for equal width intervals 0 < w ≤ 5, 5 < w ≤ 10, 10 < w ≤ 15 are 4, 9, and 7 respectively.
Calculate the percentage of items that have a weight w greater than 5.
exam.tip: Sum the relevant frequencies (9 + 7) and divide by total frequency.

exam.q: Complete the midpoint column for these class intervals: 0 < t ≤ 10, 10 < t ≤ 20, 20 < t ≤ 30.
exam.tip: Add lower and upper bounds and divide by 2 for each interval.

exam.q:
The histogram shows the heights of plants in a greenhouse with equal class intervals of width 5 cm starting from 0 cm.
The heights of bars are: 0 to 5 cm (freq 3), 5 to 10 cm (freq 8), 10 to 15 cm (freq 11), 15 to 20 cm (freq 4).
How many plants were measured in total?
exam.tip: Read the height of each bar on the y-axis and add them up.

exam.q:
The table gives information about the distance, d miles, 50 workers travel to work:
0 < d ≤ 5 (Freq 10), 5 < d ≤ 10 (Freq 18), 10 < d ≤ 15 (Freq 14), 15 < d ≤ 20 (Freq 8).
Calculate an estimate for the mean distance.
exam.tip: Show full column calculations for midpoints and (f × m) to secure method marks even if a arithmetic error occurs.

exam.q: Explain why your answer to calculating the mean from a grouped frequency table is an estimate.
model: The exact raw data values within each class interval are unknown.
exam.tip: Use key words: 'exact values are unknown' or 'we only know intervals, not exact data'.

exam.q: Describe two differences between a bar chart for discrete data and an equal-width histogram for continuous data.
model: 1. Bar charts have gaps between bars, whereas histograms have touching bars with no gaps.
2. Bar charts display discrete/categorical data, whereas histograms display continuous data on a number line scale.
exam.tip: State clearly one structural difference (gaps) and one data type difference (discrete vs continuous).

exam.q:
A student draws a histogram for data grouped as 0 < x ≤ 10 (freq 6), 10 < x ≤ 20 (freq 14), 20 < x ≤ 30 (freq 10), 30 < x ≤ 40 (freq 4).
Calculate the fraction of the total frequency represented by the interval 10 < x ≤ 20. Give your answer in simplest form.
exam.tip: Always check if the fraction can be simplified (14/34 reduces to 7/17).

worked.q:
The table below gives information about the mass, m grams, of 80 objects.

Mass (m grams) | Frequency
0 < m ≤ 20     | 12
20 < m ≤ 40    | 28
40 < m ≤ 60    | 24
60 < m ≤ 80    | 16

(a) Write down the modal class.
(b) Calculate an estimate for the mean mass.
steps: Step 1 (Modal Class): Look for the highest frequency in the table. The highest frequency is 28. The corresponding class interval is 20 < m ≤ 40.

Step 2 (Midpoints): Calculate the midpoint (m) of each class interval:
  - 0 < m ≤ 20: (0 + 20) ÷ 2 = 10
  - 20 < m ≤ 40: (20 + 40) ÷ 2 = 30
  - 40 < m ≤ 60: (40 + 60) ÷ 2 = 50
  - 60 < m ≤ 80: (60 + 80) ÷ 2 = 70

Step 3 (f × m products): Multiply each midpoint by its frequency:
  - 12 × 10 = 120
  - 28 × 30 = 840
  - 24 × 50 = 1200
  - 16 × 70 = 1120

Step 4 (Sum of f × m): Add all products together:
  - Total (f × m) = 120 + 840 + 1200 + 1120 = 3280

Step 5 (Sum of frequencies): Confirm total frequency Σf:
  - Total Frequency = 12 + 28 + 24 + 16 = 80

Step 6 (Divide): Divide total (f × m) by total frequency:
  - Estimated Mean = 3280 ÷ 80 = 41 grams
worked.ans:
(a) Modal class = 20 < m ≤ 40
(b) Estimated mean = 41 grams

worked.q:
A group of 40 students completed a puzzle. The times taken, t seconds, are recorded below:
0 < t ≤ 30 (freq 6), 30 < t ≤ 60 (freq 14), 60 < t ≤ 90 (freq 15), 90 < t ≤ 120 (freq 5).

(a) Confirm that all class intervals have equal widths.
(b) Describe how to draw the equal-width histogram on a grid.
steps:
Step 1: Calculate each class width:
  - Interval 1: 30 - 0 = 30
  - Interval 2: 60 - 30 = 30
  - Interval 3: 90 - 60 = 30
  - Interval 4: 120 - 90 = 30
  All class widths equal 30 seconds, so they are equal.

Step 2: Set up axes:
  - Horizontal axis: Label 'Time (t seconds)' with a continuous scale from 0 to 120 marked in intervals of 30.
  - Vertical axis: Label 'Frequency' with a linear scale from 0 to 16.

Step 3: Draw bars:
  - Bar 1: from x = 0 to 30, height = 6
  - Bar 2: from x = 30 to 60, height = 14
  - Bar 3: from x = 60 to 90, height = 15
  - Bar 4: from x = 90 to 120, height = 5
  Ensure all bars touch with zero space between them.
worked.ans:
(a) Yes, all class widths equal 30 seconds.
(b) Plot continuous horizontal scale 0-120, label y-axis 'Frequency' 0-16, draw touching bars of widths 30 and heights 6, 14, 15, and 5.

maths_aqa_f.5.0.summary: Mastering the concepts of populations, samples, and statistical inference is essential for interpreting data correctly in GCSE Mathematics. This guide covers why we use samples instead of whole populations, how to estimate totals using proportional scaling, and the inherent limitations and biases of sampling. Understanding these principles ensures you can evaluate claims and data reliability accurately in exams.

core.p: In statistics, we must be very precise about the group of items or people we are studying. Distinguishing between the entire group and a subset of that group is the foundation of all data collection and analysis.
bullets: A **population** is the entire collection of items, objects, or individuals that you want to study.
A **sample** is a smaller, manageable subset chosen from the population to represent it.
Studying an entire population is called a **census**.
We use a sample because a census is often too expensive, time-consuming, or physically impossible (e.g., testing every lightbulb's lifespan destroys the product).

callouts.p: The complete set of all items or individuals of interest in a statistical study.
A sample is used to make estimates and inferences about the wider population when a census is impractical.

core.p: Deciding whether to collect data from everyone or just a few requires weighing up practical constraints against statistical accuracy.
bullets: **Census advantages**: Gives completely accurate, exact data for every single member of the population with no estimation errors.
**Census disadvantages**: Takes a huge amount of time, costs a lot of money, and is impossible if testing is destructive.
**Sample advantages**: Much quicker, cheaper, and easier to manage.
**Sample disadvantages**: Only gives an estimate, and results can be prone to **sampling bias** if not chosen carefully.

callouts.p: If testing destroys the item (like checking car crash safety or firework fuses), a census is impossible because nothing would be left!

core.p: One of the main tasks at Foundation tier is using sample data to make predictions about a whole population using proportional scaling.
bullets: The formula to estimate a population total is: (Number in sample with a feature / Total sample size) multiplied by Total population size.
Alternatively, set up a proportion: (Sample count / Sample size) = (Estimated total / Population size).
Always round your final estimated answer sensibly (e.g., to the nearest whole person or object).
Never claim the estimate is an exact fact; use phrases like **'estimate'** or **'expected'**.

callouts.p: Estimate = (Sample Feature / Sample Size) x Population Size

core.p: A sample must reflect the wider population accurately. If certain groups are over-represented or under-represented, the sample is biased.
bullets: **Sampling bias** occurs when the method of choosing the sample causes certain members of the population to be less or more likely to be included.
Example of bias: Surveying people at a gym about their fitness levels gives an overly optimistic view of the town's health.
Example of bias: Asking people leaving a luxury car dealership about their income.
A **random sample** gives every single member of the population an equal chance of being selected, which minimizes bias.

callouts.p: A systematic distortion in data collection that leads to results that are unrepresentative of the true population.

core.p: Even when collected carefully, samples have inherent limitations that examiners love to test.
bullets: **Sampling variability**: Different samples taken from the same population will give different results (e.g., sample A might find 12% defectives, sample B might find 15%).
**Sample size impact**: Smaller samples are more affected by chance and outliers, leading to unreliable estimates.
**Larger samples** give more reliable and accurate estimates, but take more time and money.
A sample can never give 100% certainty about a population unless it includes everyone (a census).

callouts.p: Never say a small sample is 'wrong'—it's just less reliable and more prone to variation than a larger sample.

core.p: Exams award marks for precise justification when discussing why a sample may not be reliable. Learn these exact phrases.
bullets: 'The sample is **too small** to be representative.'
'The sample may be **biased** because...' (always state the specific context, e.g., 'only surveyed people at one store').
'Different samples would give **different results** due to sampling variability.'
'You cannot reliably apply results from one group to a **different population**.'

callouts.p: When a question asks 'Give one reason why this sample may not be reliable', always mention sample size or bias.

core.p: To avoid human choice and bias, statisticians rely on randomness.
bullets: In a true random sample, every individual has an **equal chance** of selection.
Common random methods: assigning numbers to every population member and using a **random number generator** or drawing names from a hat.
Convenience sampling (asking the first 10 people who walk past) is **not** random and almost always introduces bias.

callouts.p: A sample selected in such a way that every possible sample of the same size has an equal chance of being chosen.

core.h: 8. Interpreting Two-Way Tables and Frequency Trees with Samples
core.p: Sometimes exam questions present sample data inside tables or frequency trees and ask you to make inferences.
bullets: Always check whether the data given represents the **sample** or the **population**.
Use the sample ratio to scale up to the total population size given in the stem of the question.
Watch out for incomplete data where you must calculate missing totals first.

callouts.p: Ratio in sample = Ratio in population (assuming a representative sample was taken).

core.p: Recognising the style of question helps you secure full marks quickly.
bullets: **Type 1**: Estimate a population total using a capture-recapture or ratio method.
**Type 2**: Critique a sampling method (identify why it is biased).
**Type 3**: Explain why a sample size needs to be larger or smaller.
**Type 4**: Comment on whether a conclusion drawn from a sample is valid.

callouts.p: Always check denominators when calculating proportions from tables before scaling up.

core.p: Grade 9 questions often present a statement made by a company or politician and ask you to evaluate it using statistical reasoning.
bullets: Check if the sample size is stated. If missing or tiny, challenge the reliability.
Check who was surveyed. If the group is restricted (e.g., only teenagers, only gym members), explain why it doesn't represent the whole public.
Conclude clearly: state whether the claim is **supported** or **unsupported** and give your statistical reason.

callouts.p: Be careful with words like 'proves'. Samples provide evidence or estimates, rarely absolute proof.

analogy.p: Imagine cooking a massive pot of vegetable soup for a party. To check if there is enough salt, you don't need to eat the entire pot (a census, which would leave no soup for guests!). Instead, you stir the pot thoroughly and take one spoonful (a sample). If that spoonful tastes right, you infer the whole pot is seasoned correctly. However, if you didn't stir properly, your spoonful might be all broth with no salt, leading to a false conclusion (bias). Furthermore, taking just one tiny drop isn't enough (too small a sample size). Where the analogy breaks down is that soup is uniform if stirred well, whereas human populations have complex, diverse subgroups that are much harder to represent perfectly.

terms.d: The complete set of all items or individuals of interest in a statistical investigation.
A smaller, representative subset of a population chosen to gather data.
An official count or survey where data is collected from every single member of the population.
A systematic error where certain members of a population are improperly over-represented or under-represented.
A sample where every member of the population has an equal and independent chance of being selected.
Using sample ratios to estimate values for the wider population.
The natural variation of results obtained from different samples taken from the same population.
A sample that accurately mirrors the key characteristics and proportions of the wider population.
The consistency of results; a reliable sample produces similar estimates if repeated.
An educated calculation or approximation based on available sample data.
A method used to estimate wildlife population sizes by tagging and resampling.
Selecting a sample based on ease of access rather than randomness, highly prone to bias.

mistakes.w: Saying a sample gives the exact, true number for the population.
mistakes.r: A sample only gives an estimate, not an exact figure.

mistakes.w: Stating that a small sample is 'wrong'.
mistakes.r: A small sample is not mathematically 'wrong', but it is less reliable and more prone to sampling variability.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to scale up correctly when estimating population totals.
mistakes.r: Always multiply the sample proportion by the total population size, not just the sample size.

mistakes.w: Saying 'everyone was asked' when a sample was used.
mistakes.r: Check the wording: if only some people were asked, it is a sample, not a census.

mistakes.w: Providing vague criticisms like 'the data is bad' or 'people lied'.
mistakes.r: Give specific statistical reasons such as sample size being too small or the sampling method being biased.

mistakes.w: Confusing sample size with population size.
mistakes.r: Sample size (n) is the subset; population size (N) is the total group.

mistakes.w: Assuming a survey of 100 people from a school represents all schools nationally.
mistakes.r: Results cannot be generalised to a different population group.

exam.q: A factory makes 10,000 lightbulbs. A random sample of 50 bulbs is tested, and 2 are found to be faulty. Estimate the total number of faulty bulbs in the whole batch of 10,000.
exam.tip: Set up your sample proportion as a fraction before multiplying by the population total.

exam.q: Give one reason why a sample of 5 people is not suitable to estimate the favourite subject of all students in a secondary school.
model: The sample size is too small to be representative.
exam.tip: Always link small sample size directly to lack of representativeness.

exam.q: A researcher stands outside a golf club on a Sunday morning and asks 50 people if they support building a new sports center. Explain why this sample is biased.
model: People at a golf club are already interested in sports/recreation.
They do not represent the views of the general public.
exam.tip: Identify who was asked and why their specific viewpoint differs from the general population.

exam.q: A wildlife ranger wants to estimate the number of deer in a forest. She catches 40 deer, tags them, and releases them. Later, she catches 50 deer and finds 4 of them have tags. Estimate the total deer population.
exam.tip: Use the capture-recapture proportion: (tagged in sample 1 / total population) = (tagged in sample 2 / total in sample 2).

exam.q: A survey of 200 teenagers finds that 140 prefer online shopping to high street shops. Estimate how many teenagers out of a town population of 15,000 prefer online shopping.
exam.tip: Simplify the fraction first (140/200 = 7/10) to make multiplication easier.

exam.q: State two limitations of using sample data to make inferences about a population.
model: Results are only estimates / subject to sampling variability.
The sample might be biased and not truly representative.
exam.tip: Give two distinct statistical points: one about variability/estimates, one about bias.

exam.q: A student says, 'My sample of 10 people showed 60% like math, so exactly 60% of the entire country likes math.' Critique this statement.
model: The sample size of 10 is far too small.
The statement claims an exact figure when sample data only provides an estimate.
exam.tip: Challenge both the sample size and the misuse of the word 'exactly'.

exam.q: Why might a company choose to take a sample rather than a census when testing the lifespan of new batteries?
model: Testing batteries until they die destroys them.
A census would leave no batteries left to sell.
exam.tip: Mention destructive testing for full marks.

exam.q: Describe how a researcher could select a random sample of 20 students from a register of 200 students.
model: Assign each student a number from 1 to 200.
Use a random number generator to select 20 unique numbers.
exam.tip: Always include numbering the population and using a random selection method.

worked.q: A packet of sweets contains different colours. A random sample of 40 sweets is taken. There are 9 red sweets. (a) Estimate the probability of choosing a red sweet. (b) If there are 800 sweets in total in production, estimate how many red sweets there are.
steps: (a) Probability estimate = Number of red sweets in sample / Total sample size = 9 / 40.
(b) Scale up the sample proportion to the population total: (9 / 40) x 800.

worked.q: A local council wants to know if residents support a new recycling scheme. They survey 50 people who live on Green Lane. (a) Give one reason why this sample might not be representative of the whole town. (b) Suggest a better way to select the sample.
steps: (a) Identify the specific bias: surveying only one street (Green Lane) means residents might share similar views, socioeconomic status, or local conditions not reflective of the whole town.
(b) State a valid random sampling improvement: Obtain a complete list of all residents in the town and use a random number generator to select a random sample across all areas.
worked.ans: (a) The sample is biased because it only covers one street. (b) Use a random sample drawn from a complete list of all town residents.

maths_aqa_f.5.4.summary: Applying statistics to describe a population involves using sample data to make valid inferences, estimates, and comparisons about a larger whole. At Foundation tier, you must understand how to estimate totals using proportions, interpret basic survey data, recognise bias in sampling, and calculate expected frequencies. Master these techniques to secure top marks on practical data interpretation questions across all three GCSE papers.

core.p: In statistics, the population is the entire collection of objects, animals, or people that you want to study. Because studying an entire population is often impossible, impractical, or too expensive, we collect data from a smaller, representative subset called a sample.
bullets: **Population**: The complete set of all items or individuals of interest.
**Sample**: A smaller, manageable subset chosen from the population.
**Census**: A survey that collects data from every single member of the population.

callouts.p: The entire group of items or individuals about which we want to draw conclusions.
Never say a census is used when time and money are limited; a census takes more time and money!

core.p: You can use information gathered from a small sample to estimate the total count or numerical value for an entire population, provided the sample is unbiased and truly representative.
bullets: Find the proportion or mean from the sample data.
Multiply the sample proportion by the total population size.
Assume the sample characteristics reflect the whole population evenly.

callouts.p: Estimated Total = (Number in sample with feature / Total sample size) x Total population.

core.p: A special technique used to estimate animal or insect population sizes where direct counting is impossible. Animals are captured, marked, released, and later recaptured.
bullets: Step 1: Capture a sample, mark them harmlessly, and release them back (M).
Step 2: Later, capture a second sample (N).
Step 3: Count how many in the second sample are marked (n).
Step 4: Use the proportion M / Total = n / N to estimate the total population.

callouts.p: Estimated Population = (First marked x Second sample size) / Number recaptured marked.

core.p: Bias occurs when certain members of a population are systematically more likely to be chosen in a sample than others. This leads to inaccurate estimates of the population.
bullets: **Sampling Bias**: The sampling frame does not truly reflect the population.
**Response Bias**: Survey questions are leading or respondents do not tell the truth.
**Selection Bias**: Only people who feel strongly about the topic respond.

callouts.p: Never say a sample is biased just because it is small. It is biased if it is unrepresentative or unrandom.

core.p: To remove bias, statisticians use random sampling where every single member of the population has an exactly equal and independent chance of being selected.
bullets: Assign every member of the population a unique number.
Use a random number generator or lottery draw to pick numbers.
Ensure no human preference influences who is chosen.

callouts.p: In exams, always state 'every member has an equal chance of being selected' to gain full marks.

core.p: Expected frequency is the number of times you expect a specific outcome to occur based on probability, calculated from sample proportions applied over multiple trials.
bullets: Calculate the probability of an event from sample data.
Multiply this probability by the total number of future trials.
Expected Frequency = P(event) x Number of Trials.

callouts.p: The predicted number of times an outcome will occur in a given number of trials.

core.p: No sample is ever 100% identical to the population it represents. Understanding sampling limitations helps evaluate how trustworthy an estimate is.
bullets: Samples are only estimates; they contain natural sampling variation.
Small sample sizes lead to high variability and unreliable conclusions.
Large sample sizes reduce error but cost more time and money.

callouts.p: To make an estimate more reliable, increase the sample size and ensure it is chosen randomly.

core.p: Two-way tables categorize population data by two different variables simultaneously, making it easy to find conditional proportions and sub-population estimates.
bullets: Rows represent one variable (e.g., gender).
Columns represent another variable (e.g., pet ownership).
Totals allow you to calculate specific probabilities for sub-groups.

callouts.p: Always check that row totals match column totals for the grand total in the bottom-right corner.

core.p: When collecting data from a population, questionnaire design is critical to avoid skewed results. Questions must be unambiguous and include non-overlapping response boxes.
bullets: Avoid leading questions that push the respondent toward a specific answer.
Use checkboxes with clear, non-overlapping numerical intervals.
Provide an 'Other' or catch-all category where appropriate.

callouts.p: Avoid ambiguous intervals like 1-10, 10-20. Where does 10 go? Use 1-10, 11-20 instead.

core.p: Exam questions often present a statement made about a population based on a small study. You must critically analyze whether the data supports the claim.
bullets: Check if the sample was large enough to make a sweeping claim.
Look for hidden bias or flaws in the data collection method.
State clearly whether the claim is justified and give a mathematical reason.

callouts.p: When asked 'Is Jim correct?', always start your answer with 'No, because...' followed by evidence from the data.

core.p: When population probabilities are unknown, we use relative frequency from experimental data as the best estimate for the true probability.
bullets: Relative Frequency = (Frequency of successful outcomes) / (Total number of trials)
As the number of trials increases, relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability.
This principle is known as the Law of Large Numbers.

callouts.p: An estimate of probability based on the results of actual experiments or surveys.

core.h: 12. Putting It All Together: Population Reports
core.p: Top-grade exam questions combine estimation, ratio, and percentage skills into multi-step problems describing an entire population from sample statistics.
bullets: Identify the sample ratio or percentage given.
Set up a direct proportion equation with the population total.
Check your final answer for common sense and correct units.

callouts.p: If your estimated number of people is a decimal, round appropriately to the nearest whole person!

analogy.t: Sampling soup vs. eating the whole pot
analogy.p: Imagine you are making a massive pot of vegetable soup for a party. To check if it has enough salt, you do not need to eat the entire pot (a census). Instead, you stir it well, take one single spoonful (a sample), taste it, and use that to estimate the seasoning of the whole pot. This breaks down if you forget to stir the soup first: if all the salt settled at the bottom, your spoonful would be biased and give you a false impression of the whole pot.

terms.d: The entire group of items or individuals about which we want to draw conclusions.
A smaller subset selected from the population to represent it.
A survey of every single member of the population.
A systematic distortion in data collection that favors certain outcomes.
A sample where every member of the population has an equal and independent chance of being chosen.
A method used to estimate animal population sizes using marked samples.
The number of times an outcome is predicted to occur in a given number of trials.
The experimental probability calculated from actual trial results.
A complete list of all members of the population from which a sample is drawn.
Sharing the same characteristics and proportions as the wider population.
A part compared to the whole, expressed as a fraction, decimal, or percentage.
The collection of data from individuals through questions or measurements.

mistakes.w: Saying a census is quicker and cheaper than a sample.
mistakes.r: A census takes much more time, effort, and money because it questions everyone.

mistakes.w: Writing that a sample is biased because it is small.
mistakes.r: Small samples have high variability, but bias specifically means it is unrepresentative or unrandom.

mistakes.w: Leaving an estimated number of people as a decimal like 45.6 people.
mistakes.r: Round discrete real-world counts like people or animals to the nearest whole number.

mistakes.w: Using overlapping intervals like 1-10, 10-20 in a questionnaire.
mistakes.r: Intervals must be non-overlapping, such as 1-10, 11-20.

mistakes.w: Assuming a sample perfectly mirrors the population without any error.
mistakes.r: Samples always contain natural sampling variation and are only estimates.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply back by the total population when scaling up proportions.
mistakes.r: Always multiply the sample fraction by the entire population size to get the estimated total.

mistakes.w: Writing 'everyone had a chance' for random sampling.
mistakes.r: Must specify 'an EQUAL chance' of being selected.

exam.q: A school has 1200 pupils. A sample of 60 pupils is surveyed. 15 of them walk to school. Estimate how many pupils in the whole school walk to school.
exam.tip: Find the sample fraction first, then multiply by the total population.

exam.q: Explain why a survey of 50 people leaving a gym is not a suitable sample to estimate the fitness levels of all adults in a town.
model: It is biased because people at a gym are already fitter than average.
It does not represent the whole town.
exam.tip: Always mention bias and lack of representation.

exam.q: A biologist catches 40 fish from a lake, marks them, and releases them. Later, she catches 50 fish and finds that 8 of them are marked. Estimate the total number of fish in the lake.
exam.tip: Use the capture-recapture proportion formula carefully.

exam.q: Give two reasons why a census might not be used instead of a sample.
model: Too expensive / costs too much money.
Takes too long / impractical for large populations.
Destructive testing makes a census impossible (any two valid points).
exam.tip: Learn standard justifications for sampling over censuses.

exam.q: State what is meant by a random sample.
model: Every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
exam.tip: Must include the word 'equal'.

exam.q: A bag contains red and blue counters. In 20 trials, a red counter is picked 12 times. Estimate the probability of picking a blue counter.
exam.tip: Remember probabilities sum to 1.

exam.q: A town council wants to know if residents support building a new park. They survey 100 people at a local tennis club. Criticize this sample.
model: Tennis club members are more likely to want outdoor/sports facilities than the general public.
exam.tip: Link the specific location of the survey to the specific topic asked.

exam.q: In a survey, a question asks: 'Don't you agree that tax is too high?' Explain why this question is biased.
exam.tip: Identify leading questions instantly in exam contexts.

exam.q: A factory produces 10,000 light bulbs per day. A random sample of 200 bulbs is tested, and 3 are found to be faulty. Estimate how many faulty bulbs are produced in a day.
exam.tip: Scale sample rate directly to total daily production.

worked.q: A wildlife park has an estimated deer population. 60 deer are captured, tagged, and released. Two weeks later, a sample of 80 deer is captured, and 12 are found to have tags. Calculate the estimated total population of deer in the park.
steps: Identify the variables: First marked (M) = 60, Second sample size (N) = 80, Recaptured marked (n) = 12.
Set up the proportion: Marked in sample / Total in second sample = Total marked / Total population, so 12 / 80 = 60 / Total.
Rearrange to solve for Total: Total = (60 x 80) / 12.
Calculate value: 4800 / 12 = 400.

worked.q: A market researcher surveys a random sample of 150 people in a city of 45,000 people. 42 people say they cycle to work. Estimate how many people in the city cycle to work.
steps: Find the sample proportion: 42 / 150.
Simplify or convert to decimal: 42 / 150 = 0.28.
Multiply by the total population: 0.28 x 45,000.
Calculate final total: 12,600.

maths_aqa_f.5.3.summary: Understanding how to compare distributions is essential for describing data sets. You must be able to calculate and interpret the mean, median, mode, range, quartiles and inter‑quartile range, and you should know how to read and construct box plots. These measures together show the centre, spread and shape of a distribution, allowing you to decide which data set is higher, more spread out or more symmetric. Mastery of these tools lets you answer exam questions that ask you to compare two or more groups of numbers accurately and efficiently.

core.p: A distribution shows how a set of values is spread out. It can be displayed in a table, a list, a diagram or a box plot. The key is to see where the data cluster and how far they extend.
bullets: All values belong to the same variable (e.g. test scores).
The order of the values does not matter for most measures.
A distribution can be symmetric, skewed left or skewed right.

callouts.p: A set of data values shown together to illustrate how they are spread.

core.p: The mean is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values. It gives the *balance point* of the distribution.
bullets: Formula: \(\bar{x}=\frac{\sum x}{n}\)
Add all the numbers, then divide by the count.
Use a calculator for large data sets.

callouts.p: The mean is sensitive to extreme values (outliers).
Check your total before dividing – a common slip is to forget a value.

fig.cap: Mean as the balance point of a seesaw diagram.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="50" y="100" width="300" height="20" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="190" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Mean</text></svg>

core.p: The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest. If there is an even number of values, the median is the average of the two central numbers.
bullets: Arrange data in ascending order.
If n is odd, median = value at position \((n+1)/2\).
If n is even, median = average of values at positions \(n/2\) and \(n/2+1\).

callouts.p: The middle value of an ordered data set; 50% of the data lie below and 50% above.
Do NOT use the mean when the question asks for the median.

fig.cap: Box plot showing the median as the line inside the box.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="120" y="100" width="160" height="40" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><line x1="200" y1="100" x2="200" y2="140" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="190" y="95" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Median</text></svg>

core.p: The mode is the value(s) that occur most frequently. A distribution can have no mode, one mode (unimodal) or more than one mode (bimodal, multimodal).
bullets: Count how many times each value occurs.
The highest frequency gives the mode.
If all frequencies are equal, there is no mode.

callouts.p: The most frequently occurring value(s) in a data set.

core.p: The range measures the total spread of the data. It is the difference between the largest and smallest values.
bullets: Formula: \\(\\text{Range}=\\text{Maximum}-\\text{Minimum}\\)
Quick way to see how far the data extend.
Does not give any information about the values in between.

callouts.p: Range is highly affected by outliers.

fig.cap: Number line showing minimum, maximum and the range.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="50" y1="120" x2="350" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540"/><circle cx="100" cy="120" r="5" fill="#bbf7d0"/><circle cx="300" cy="120" r="5" fill="#bbf7d0"/><text x="90" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Min</text><text x="290" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Max</text><text x="200" y="140" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Range = Max‑Min</text></svg>

core.p: Quartiles split an ordered data set into four equal parts. Q1 (lower quartile) is the median of the lower half, Q2 is the median of the whole set, and Q3 (upper quartile) is the median of the upper half.
bullets: Arrange data in order.
Find the median (Q2).
For Q1, take the lower half (excluding Q2 if n is odd) and find its median.
For Q3, take the upper half and find its median.
Quartiles give a picture of the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

callouts.p: Values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts.
Do not include the overall median when n is odd while finding Q1 and Q3.

core.p: The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data. It is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles.
bullets: Formula: \\(\\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1\\)
Ignores extreme values, so it is robust against outliers.
Used to construct box plots and to detect outliers (values > 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles).

callouts.p: IQR is the length of the box in a box plot.

core.p: A box plot visualises the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum. It shows the centre, spread and any potential outliers.
bullets: Step 1: Order the data.
Step 2: Find the minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
Step 3: Draw a number line covering the range.
Step 4: Mark the five numbers on the line.
Step 5: Draw a box from Q1 to Q3 and a line inside at the median.
Step 6: Extend ‘whiskers’ to the minimum and maximum (or to 1.5 × IQR if outliers are to be shown).

callouts.p: Label the axes clearly and use the same scale for all parts of the plot.

fig.cap: Complete box plot with whiskers, box and median line.

core.p: When asked to compare, look at the five‑number summary and the mean/median. Decide which is higher, which is more spread out and whether one is more symmetric.
bullets: Higher mean/median → higher centre.
Larger range or IQR → more spread.
If the median is close to the mean, the distribution is roughly symmetric.
Box plots make visual comparison quick.

callouts.p: Always state which measure you are using when you say ‘higher’ or ‘more spread’.

core.p: A‑level exam questions use precise wording. Recognise key command words and what they ask you to do.
bullets: "State the mean/median" – give the numerical value.
"Compare the spreads" – discuss range and IQR.
"Explain which distribution is more symmetric" – refer to the closeness of mean and median.
"Construct a box plot" – follow the five‑step method.

callouts.p: Do not mix up ‘range’ with ‘inter‑quartile range’; they are different measures.

analogy.t: Box plot as a school timetable
analogy.p: Imagine a school timetable where the earliest lesson start time is the minimum, the latest finish time is the maximum, the lunch break marks the median, and the start and end of the morning and afternoon sessions are Q1 and Q3. The length of the lunch break (IQR) shows how much of the day is spent in the middle of the schedule. The analogy breaks down because a timetable is ordered by time, not by the size of lesson lengths, and it does not show outliers like an unexpected extra lesson.

terms.d: The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The middle value of an ordered data set; 50% of the data lie below and 50% above.
The most frequently occurring value(s) in a data set.
Maximum value minus minimum value.
Values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts (Q1, Q2, Q3).
The difference between the upper and lower quartiles (Q3‑Q1).
A diagram showing the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum of a data set.
The set {minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum}.
A value that lies more than 1.5 × IQR beyond Q1 or Q3.
A distribution where the mean and median are close together.
A distribution with a longer tail on the left; median > mean.
A distribution with a longer tail on the right; mean > median.

mistakes.w: Using the mean when the question asks for the median.
mistakes.r: The mark scheme expects the median; the mean is a different measure.

mistakes.w: Including the overall median when calculating Q1 and Q3 for an odd‑sized data set.
mistakes.r: Do not count the median in either half when n is odd.

mistakes.w: Confusing range with inter‑quartile range.
mistakes.r: Range = max‑min; IQR = Q3‑Q1.

mistakes.w: Writing ‘mode is the average’.
mistakes.r: The mode is the most frequent value, not an average.

mistakes.w: Leaving the whiskers of a box plot at the minimum and maximum even when outliers exist.
mistakes.r: Whiskers should stop at 1.5 × IQR; outliers are plotted separately.

mistakes.w: Stating ‘higher spread’ without specifying whether you mean range or IQR.
mistakes.r: Specify the measure you are comparing.

mistakes.w: Mis‑reading Q1 as the first value in the data set.
mistakes.r: Q1 is the median of the lower half, not the first data point.

mistakes.w: Adding the median twice when finding the total for the mean.
mistakes.r: The median is not part of the sum for the mean.

mistakes.w: Using a histogram instead of a box plot when the question asks for a box plot.
mistakes.r: Follow the required diagram type.

mistakes.w: Failing to label the axes or scale on a box plot.
mistakes.r: Clear labeling is required for full marks.

exam.q: The test scores for Class A are: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 24. State the mean, median and mode.
model: Ordered data: 12,15,15,18,20,22,24 → median is the 4th value = 18
Mode = 15 (appears twice, more than any other value)
exam.tip: Check the total carefully; the median is the centre value when n is odd.

exam.q: For the data set {5, 7, 9, 12, 14, 16, 20, 22}, find Q1, Q2, Q3 and the inter‑quartile range.
exam.tip: When n is even, split the data into two equal halves before finding Q1 and Q3.

exam.q: The following box plot shows the weekly hours spent on homework by two year‑12 groups. Group X: min 2, Q1 4, median 6, Q3 9, max 12. Group Y: min 3, Q1 5, median 7, Q3 8, max 10. Compare the spreads of the two groups.
model: Range X = 12‑2 = 10, Range Y = 10‑3 = 7 → X has a larger range.
IQR X = 9‑4 = 5, IQR Y = 8‑5 = 3 → X is more spread in the middle 50%.
Therefore Group X is more spread overall than Group Y.
exam.tip: State both range and IQR to justify your comparison.

exam.q: Construct a box plot for the data: 4, 8, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 22, 25.
model: Draw number line 0‑30, mark 4, 8.5, 13, 20, 25, draw box from 8.5 to 20, line at 13, whiskers to 4 and 25.
exam.tip: Label each part of the box plot clearly; use the five‑number summary.

exam.q: Explain why the mean is not always the best measure of centre for a skewed distribution.
model: The mean is pulled towards the tail of a skewed distribution, so it does not represent the typical value as well as the median.
exam.tip: Use the terms ‘skewed’, ‘tail’ and ‘typical value’.

exam.q: A data set has a mean of 30, a median of 28 and a mode of 25. Comment on the shape of the distribution.
model: Mean > median > mode indicates a right‑skewed (positively skewed) distribution.
The tail is on the right side, pulling the mean up.
exam.tip: Recall the order of centre measures for skewness.

exam.q: Identify any outliers in the data set {3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 28}. Use the 1.5 × IQR rule.
exam.tip: Show each calculation step for full marks.

exam.q: State the five‑number summary for the data: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16.
exam.tip: Remember Q1 and Q3 are medians of the lower and upper halves.

exam.q: Two classes have the following means and ranges: Class A – mean 65, range 20; Class B – mean 68, range 12. Which class performed better overall? Justify your answer.
model: Class B has a higher mean, indicating a higher overall centre.
Class A has a larger range, showing more variation.
If ‘better overall’ refers to higher achievement, Class B performed better because of the higher mean.
exam.tip: State which measure you are using to decide ‘better’.

exam.q: Explain how a box plot can help you identify the symmetry of a distribution.
model: If the median is centred in the box and the whiskers are of similar length, the distribution is roughly symmetric; unequal whisker lengths indicate skewness.
exam.tip: Mention the position of the median within the box.

worked.q: Find the mean, median, mode, range and IQR for the data set: 3, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18.
steps: Order the data (already ordered).
Median = 4th value = 9.
Mode = 7 (appears twice).
Q1 = median of {3,7,7} = 7.

worked.q: Construct a box plot for the data: 5, 8, 11, 14, 18, 22, 27, 30.
steps: Minimum = 5, Maximum = 30.
Draw a number line covering 0‑35.
Draw box from 9.5 to 24.5, line at 16, whiskers to 5 and 30.
worked.ans: Box plot with min = 5, Q1 = 9.5, median = 16, Q3 = 24.5, max = 30
